subject: Start Here: Business Model Mastery is evolving to help you build your investable universe
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://bizmodelmastery.substack.com/p/start-here-business-model-mastery

Business Model Mastery is the free daily newsletter by The Antifragile Investor, trusted by 7,000+ long-term investors across 120+ countries.
It is built for long-term investors who want to understand high-quality listed businesses, compare great business models, and build a mental database of companies they may feel comfortable owning for many years at the right price.
This is not a place for hot tickers, trading calls, or easy-money promises.
It is for people who want to understand the business beneath the stock before they ever think about owning it.
That distinction matters.
A watchlist is just a list of names. An investable universe is different. It is a group of businesses you understand well enough to compare, monitor, judge, and potentially own for a long time.
That is what Business Model Mastery exists to help you build.
Not a random collection of stocks, but a growing map of great business models, durable advantages, cash-flow patterns, risks, key metrics, and ownership-quality companies.
For the last six months, Business Model Mastery worked in a focused way: one company each week, studied from different angles across the week.
That format was useful. It gave us time to stay with one business long enough to understand how it made money, why customers paid, what protected its economics, where the risks were, and which numbers mattered most.
Now Business Model Mastery is evolving.
The previous version helped us spend more time with one company. The new version will help you move across more industries, more countries, more company sizes, more business models, more competitive advantages, and more cash-flow patterns.
The goal is not “more companies.”
The goal is better business judgment.
Every day, one listed company becomes a practical case for understanding one business model, one advantage or weakness, one key number, and one lesson you can use again when studying other companies.
Some companies will be large global leaders. Others may be smaller, less obvious businesses.
The reason to study them will be the same: they teach something worth knowing about how strong businesses make money, defend their position, and create value over time.
Think of Business Model Mastery as something more useful than a traditional MBA for long-term investors.
Not a formal degree. Not academic theory. Not classroom cases detached from the market.
A practical education in listed businesses: actual companies, actual numbers, actual business models, actual competitive advantages, actual tradeoffs, and actual investment alternatives you can compare.
The goal is not to sound smart about business.
The goal is to understand enough to make better long-term decisions.
Because if you invest in individual companies, one thing is unavoidable: you need to understand what you might own.
If you do not understand the business beneath the stock, you are mostly reacting to price, news, charts, valuation multiples, and other people’s opinions.
That is not the kind of investing I want to help you practice.
Business Model Mastery is for people who want to understand the business first: how it earns money, why customers keep paying, how it competes, what could damage the model, and which numbers tell you whether the thesis is still working.
This matters because the final goal is not excitement.
It is not constant activity. It is not finding the next stock to talk about.
The final goal is peace of mind built on understanding.
If you know how a company makes money, what protects it, what could hurt it, which KPI matters, and what would make you change your mind, you are in a very different position from someone simply holding a ticker.
You can still be wrong. Markets can still fall. Surprises can still happen.
But there is a huge difference between owning a business you have studied and holding a stock you barely understand.
That is the gap Business Model Mastery tries to close.
Each issue is short enough to read inside your normal day, but serious enough to compound over time.
Two minutes a day may feel small. That is the point. Small enough to keep. Strong enough to compound.
One company. One business model. One key number. One advantage or weakness. One useful lesson.
After one issue, you understand one business better. After one month, you have studied dozens of models, industries, risks, and key numbers.
After six months, you should have a much wider map of how great listed businesses actually work.
That is compound interest applied to learning.
The benefit does not come only from one article.
It comes from staying with the habit long enough that the lessons begin to connect.
You start seeing why a payment network should not be judged like a bank.
Why a luxury company should not be judged like a mass-market manufacturer. Why a marketplace can look impressive while customer acquisition costs absorb too much of the economics.
You start seeing why a distributor can report profit while inventory absorbs cash.
Why an alternative asset manager’s headline assets matter less than the capital that actually pays fees. Why some companies deserve premium valuations and others look cheap for a reason.
This is where variety matters.
If you only study one type of company, your comparisons stay weak.
A software company, a payment network, a luxury brand, an insurer, a distributor, an exchange, and a serial acquirer do not create value in the same way.
They have different economics, different risks, different cash-flow patterns, different ways of building advantage, and different ways of failing.
Business Model Mastery helps you compare them properly.
You begin to ask better questions: Is this business model superior? Is the advantage visible in the numbers? Is growth making the company better, or only larger? Does profit become cash? What would show that the story is breaking?
Those questions matter because investing is always comparison.
You are always choosing between this company and that company, this business model and another one, this valuation and another use of your capital.
If you cannot compare alternatives, you cannot allocate capital well.
You may like a company, but is it better than another high-quality business available at a similar price?
You may find a stock cheap, but is it cheap because the market is wrong, or because the business is getting worse?
You may admire a company’s growth, but is that growth creating owner value, or only making the company bigger?
Business Model Mastery is built to help you develop the judgment to answer those questions.
Every issue starts with the business itself: how does this company actually make money?
Not the polished company presentation. The business.
Who pays? Why do they pay? How often do they pay? What problem is being solved? Can customers delay, switch, negotiate harder, or leave without much pain?
These questions look simple. They are not.
They pull the analysis away from vague admiration and toward the economics of the business, where the useful answers usually begin.
A company can be famous, loved, fast-growing, and widely discussed. None of that is enough.
You need to understand why the business works, and just as important, what would make it stop working.
That is where competitive advantage enters.
Not as a decorative word. Not because the company is famous. Not because the chart looked good for ten years.
A competitive advantage must be proven by customer behavior and numbers.
If a brand matters, customers should pay more, wait longer, return more often, or accept limited availability.
If a network matters, more users should make the service more useful, not just larger.
If switching costs matter, customers should stay even when prices rise or cheaper alternatives appear.
If scale matters, the company should produce better economics than smaller competitors.
If trust matters, customers should keep committing money, time, or important decisions even when alternatives exist.
That is the discipline: do not admire the story before checking what customers do.
Do not call something a moat before seeing the proof.
Do not trust growth before asking what it costs.
Growth deserves special suspicion.
Not because growth is bad. Because growth is often misunderstood.
A company can grow revenue while the business becomes weaker.
It can add customers while spending more to attract them, expand through acquisitions while the core business slows, or report rising profit while receivables and inventory absorb cash.
That is why the same growth rate can mean very different things in different business models.
So Business Model Mastery will keep asking one uncomfortable question: is this company becoming better, or only bigger?
Good growth usually leaves evidence.
Margins hold or improve, cash grows with revenue, customer relationships deepen, the company becomes harder to replace, returns on capital remain attractive, and debt stays controlled.
Weak growth looks different.
More sales, but more inventory. More users, but higher marketing costs. More branches, but lower productivity. More acquisitions, but weaker organic performance. More adjusted profit, but less owner cash.
This is where many investing mistakes begin.
The story says growth. The numbers say strain.
That is why cash will stay central.
Revenue can impress. Profit can mislead. Adjusted numbers can make weak economics look cleaner than they are.
Cash forces a more honest discussion.
We will keep looking at operating cash flow, free cash flow, owner earnings, working capital, capital intensity, debt, and the spending needed to keep the business strong.
Not because accounting is the whole story.
Because a business that cannot turn its story into cash deserves more skepticism.
Not every company needs the same number.
That is the mistake in generic analysis. A serious investor learns which metric matters for each type of business.
For an alternative asset manager, the key may be fee-paying capital and recurring fee earnings, not only headline assets.
For a luxury business, the key may be scarcity, waiting time, margin, and cash, not only brand fame.
For a payment network, the key may be net revenue after incentives, not only transaction volume.
For a marketplace, the key may be cash after demand acquisition costs, not only gross bookings.
For a distributor, the key may be inventory growth versus sales, not only revenue and gross margin.
For an insurer, the key may be underwriting discipline, not only premium growth.
Different businesses require different tests.
That is the work: find the number that tells the truth for that model, then carry the lesson into the next company.
That is why each issue should leave you with one useful principle.
Not just facts. Not just data. A principle you can use again.
For an asset manager: fee-paying capital matters more than headline capital.
For a luxury business: scarcity is valuable only when demand stays deeper than supply.
For a payment network: transaction growth matters only if the company keeps enough economics after incentives.
For a marketplace: demand is valuable only when it becomes cash after acquisition costs.
For a distributor: availability matters only after inventory is funded.
For an insurer: growth is valuable only if underwriting discipline survives.
These are the kinds of lessons that make the next company easier to understand.
You study the company, but you keep the principle. And the principle makes you better the next time you see a similar business, even in another industry or another country.
This is one of the best parts of the whole process.
A lesson learned in one industry can help you understand another. A KPI studied in one company can help you ask a sharper question somewhere else.
A cash-flow pattern from one business can make a future red flag easier to notice.
That is how you prepare before the opportunity appears.
When a great business becomes available at a fair or attractive price, you do not want to start from zero.
You want to already understand the model, the advantage, the risks, the numbers, and what would make the opportunity interesting.
Business Model Mastery is built for that.
Not to give you ready-made stock tips.
Not to tell you what to buy. Not to replace your judgment.
I do not want to give you borrowed conviction.
I want to help you build your own.
That is much more valuable, because what you learn properly stays with you.
A stock tip expires. A business model learned well can serve you for years.
This is why I care so much about the daily habit.
I have spent a lot of time and money over the years trying to learn ideas that could stay useful for a long time.
The best education is not the kind that gives you a quick answer.
It is the kind that changes how you think.
That is what I want to transfer through Business Model Mastery.
Not certainty. Not predictions. Not noise.
A better way to understand businesses.
If you are here, you are probably already above average in one important way: you are trying to understand the business beneath the stock.
Not only the price. Not only the valuation. Not only the chart. Not only the latest news.
That is not easy at the beginning.
Sometimes you may not understand everything immediately. That is normal.
The point is not to understand every detail on day one.
The point is to keep showing up, keep reading, keep connecting the ideas, and let the learning compound.
The future version of you will be grateful for that.
Because the knowledge you build today can stay with you for years. And in investing, few things matter more than slowly becoming harder to fool.
That is why Business Model Mastery is meant to become a long-term habit.
Short enough to keep. Serious enough to matter. Useful enough to carry forward.
Small daily reading. Compounding business judgment. A wider investable universe.
And now there is another important part.
Business Model Mastery will stay free, and the free version will remain extremely valuable.
Even if you never decide to go to the next level, it will still help you build a list of high-quality companies, understand their business models, recognize their key metrics, and compare opportunities with more clarity.
But I am also building something much deeper.
It is called The Investable Universe Academy.
It will be the full 12-month guided journey to build your mental database of the world’s greatest business models in depth.
The idea is simple: we will spend one full year building your investable universe together, one business model, one moat, one KPI, and one decision rule at a time.
The free daily newsletter will help you build the habit and understand the foundations.
The Investable Universe Academy will be for readers who want to go much deeper and turn this daily habit into a structured long-term learning path.
It will not be a quick product for people looking for fast stock ideas.
It will be for serious long-term investors who want to understand the world’s best listed businesses in depth, compare them intelligently, and build the confidence to know what may deserve long-term ownership at the right price.
Soon, the doors will open.
If you want to know when The Investable Universe Academy becomes available, the best thing to do is simple: stay subscribed to Business Model Mastery.
This free daily newsletter will be the place where I announce the opening, explain the full path, and show you how to join when the time comes.
If you are not subscribed yet, start here. Subscribe to Business Model Mastery for free 👇🏻
The full deep dive reports are not going away.
This is important, because I know many of you have followed Business Model Mastery through those reports, and some of you may naturally wonder whether I will continue producing them.
The answer is yes.
Many of you liked them a lot, bought them, and sent me very strong feedback. I appreciate that deeply, and I will continue to produce new full deep dives when a company deserves the full treatment.
I am proud of that work.
Those reports are deep, detailed, and built for serious long-term investors who want to understand a company properly: business model, competitive advantage, management, strategy, industry dynamics, valuation, owner earnings, risks, and expected return.
The previous full deep dive reports are still available, but not at the original launch-week price.
I promised early buyers that the launch price would not come back, and I will keep that promise.
You can still buy the previous reports at the current full price.
Many of them remain highly relevant because they cover high-quality companies whose business models, competitive advantages, risks, and long-term economics are still worth understanding.
Some of those companies may go through difficult periods.
That does not automatically make the reports less useful. In some cases, difficult periods are exactly when deep business understanding becomes more valuable.
If a company has low debt, strong economics, and a better competitive position than weaker peers, a sector crisis or economic downturn may hurt competitors more severely and give the stronger business room to act in ways others cannot.
That does not mean every crisis is good.
It means the same crisis can have very different effects depending on debt, business quality, competitive position, and management discipline.
That is one of the reasons I am still proud of those reports.
They were not built around short-term excitement. They were built around the deeper questions: how does the business work, what protects it, what can hurt it, and what would make it worth serious long-term attention?
Business Model Mastery will be the place where I tell you when new full deep dive reports become available.
I am still thinking carefully about the best future format for those reports, including whether an annual full deep dive subscription makes sense.
For now, the idea is simple.
The daily newsletter helps you build the broad map. The full deep dives let you stop on selected companies and study them properly.
The previous full deep dive reports are still available.
If you want to go deeper into the companies I have already studied, you can find the full library of reports, bundles, and products here:

There is also a slower way to stay close to the work.
If one email a day is too frequent for you, The Antifragile Investor Playbook is the weekly companion.
It is built for readers who want one deeper practical piece each week instead of a daily company lesson.
It is also complementary to Business Model Mastery.
You can read both if you want the daily company lessons and the weekly thinking tools behind the analysis.
The Playbook is for readers who want to understand the logic behind company analysis: which filters matter, why they matter, how to judge cash flow, how to assess moat, how to spot accounting red flags, and how to screen a company in a few minutes before deciding whether it deserves deeper work.
In other words, Business Model Mastery helps you study businesses every day.
The Antifragile Investor Playbook helps you understand the rules behind the analysis.
The Playbook will also be another place where I share important updates about my more advanced work, new research, future products, and the bigger project I am building.
So if you want a slower pace, or if you want to sharpen the thinking behind the daily work, you should take a look.

So this is how everything fits together.
Business Model Mastery is the free daily route.
The full deep dives are still available. And I will produce more of those as well. 
The Playbook is the weekly companion.
The Investable Universe Academy is the full 12-month guided journey.
All of it serves one goal: helping you understand businesses better, compare investment alternatives more intelligently, and build your investable universe one high-quality business model at a time.
This will not be for everyone.
If you want market noise, quick trades, hot tickers, or borrowed conviction, this is probably not the right place.
If you are a trader looking for something to buy today and sell next month, this is not built for you.
There are no short-term calls here. No promise of fast money. No attempt to make investing feel easy.
But if you want to invest seriously, understand what you own, compare businesses intelligently, and build an investable universe of high-quality companies you may feel comfortable owning for many years, you are exactly where you should be.
This article will stay here as a starting point.
If you are new, start with Business Model Mastery. If you have been reading for months, this is the next phase of the same mission.
Build your investable universe, one business model at a time.
Read across industries, compare across opportunities, and keep the principles that make every future business easier to understand.
One stronger investor mind, built slowly and deliberately.
And above all: a better chance to understand what you own well enough to sleep well at night.
Soon, The Investable Universe Academy will open.
The complete 12-month guided journey where we go much deeper into the world’s greatest business models.

Keep the habit. Let it compound. It is worth it.

The Antifragile Investor

subject: How I Find Interesting Stocks
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://deepvaluecapitalbykyler.substack.com/p/how-i-find-stocks-to-invest-in

The ability to execute on a good repeatable process defines a great investing career. I have been refining and iterating mine for almost 7 years and now do this full time.
That process starts with finding opportunities. If you can’t find anything you understand you are left with bad options.
So this article is my process for finding stocks to invest in. Before we get to that process though it is worth knowing what my strategy is. 
Put as simply as possible my strategy is buying good businesses at great prices.
Businesses with long operating histories and proven track records going through temporary issues that cause them to be mispriced.
My favored method for finding new ideas that fit that strategy changes often but after lots of trial and error I believe the base will always remain.
The best way to find those good companies trading at a discount is to search among those down from highs.
So that is what I do.
I simply run a screener on Koyfin [ https://substack.com/redirect/e531aa1b-dad0-45c9-b5ad-983822c054fd?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ] every day for stocks down 50% or more from all time highs, and within 20% of 52 week lows.
You would consistently be surprised how many large and well known companies are in this bucket.
The only other filter I set on top of this is excluding those listed on exchanges I can't access.
Then I go through each name one by one.
I may have a sector or country I am interested and will focus on those but often it is literally going A-Z or large to small market cap.
There are thousands of names on the list so this can take a very long time. 
Then prices move the next day.
The fun never ends!
For now as I search through that list my process is nuanced but relatively straight forward.
Step 1: Stock Chart
Typically the first thing you see is the stock chart, and it can quickly help inform decisions.
For example how long have they been public? If it has been 20+ years I know the business has seen cycles and survived them.
Does it show massive spikes (multi 100% moves) and sell offs? Depending on the year that could mean they are a healthcare company with a business that benefited from the Covid boom, they are cyclical, or rely on commodity prices. Or if it was largely a prominent recent massive rise then decline I know it will take time build a shareholder base.
I rarely make decisions based on the chart alone when I have already filtered for those down from highs but I will pass when it is clear it is not down enough.
This happens when I see a large short lived spike well above trend followed by the decline. That pattern tells me expectations got ahead of the fundamentals and in these cases they very often need to fall significantly further than 50% to get back to reasonable valuation and time to rebuild confidence.
Step 2: Business Description
This step is straight forward, what do they do?
In the past I had filtered out industries I did not understand from the get go but I have stopped doing that because screeners don’t always get it right and it causes me to miss things. It will also force me to learn more about areas I am not as familiar with.
The whole goal of this step is to weed out those companies I obviously don’t know enough about to invest in.
Everyone’s list will be different but these are industries that are outside my circle of competence today or that I avoid due to their capital destructive nature:
Pure AI
Airlines
Banks
Biotech
Car Manufacturers
Insurance
Marine Freight
Precious Metal Miners
Restaurants
Tobacco
Textiles
Trading Firms
Most Software
Video Games
Psst, have questions? Leave a comment and I will respond to anything you ask.
Step 3: Basic Financials
After a stock has passed the first two steps I move onto the part that takes more than just a couple seconds. 
I spend a few minutes looking at their financials to determine if the company qualifies as quality and has at least some possibility of meeting my hurdle rate of return, 30%/yr.
I measure quality by the following metrics:
Returns on Capital (ROIC & ROCE)
Do they have historical returns on capital high single digits (~7%) or better most of the time? What direction are they moving?
While I do think returns on capital are important for determining if the business is good or better, it is much less make or break for my strategy than traditional value investing.
I am looking to simply weed out the terrible companies.
Growth Trend
Do they show signs of revenue growth? Or stabilization after a recent fall?
There is no specific growth level I am looking for, simply that this is not a company still in decline or shows signs of stabilizing. 
Margins
Do they have a history of being profitable?
This is an obvious one, if the company has never made money that is a good sign the future might not be much different. I look at gross margins, EBIT margins, operating cash flow margins, and free cash flow margins.
You need to get familiar with IFRS rules as they can distort what you are used to with US companies. Outside the US I have been leaning more and more on EBIT margins for my quick checks.
Dilution
Do they have a history of share buybacks? Or at least treating shareholders well? IE no constant dilution.
If they raise the share count by several percent every single year that is an immediate hit to company quality.
It tells me that management doesn’t respect shareholders but is instead lining their pockets or doing anything to keep the company alive, even if that destroys shareholder wealth. If share count is rising slowly relative to revenue I may be able to forgive but I am more critical when I see this happening.
The exception to this is acquisitions. If you see one year jumps followed by periods of flat that tells a different story. They bought out a company so check to see how per share profits are moving. 
Did they create or destroy value? How did margins and returns on capital change after the acquisitions?
If a company can pass the first half of that step with no obvious red flags I try to determine if they have a shot at meeting or exceeding my 30%/yr threshold, if they can that is what I mean by a “great price”.
I do this by looking at historical margins and valuation multiples. Estimating what a “normalized” margin and multiple might look like gives me a rough sense of whether a stock could double or more over the next 2–3 years.
I use Stock Unlock [ https://substack.com/redirect/6fb1abd8-a1b2-47e4-aa73-f1f365e4ff92?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ] to look at company financials, historical valuations, and as a home for the names I am still researching.
I chose Stock Unlock for its long term data, low cost, and access to global markets.
Today, this is my preferred way of finding ideas, though I do pull from other sources too and run them through the same steps. (Substack, YouTube, podcasts, news articles, etc.)
This whole process takes me anywhere from 5 seconds to 2 minutes depending on the stock with 98%+ not making it past them.
I only want the truly exceptional opportunities and this is designed to find them.
In 2024 that was CRK  at $8 or IHS  at $2.50. Both up over 150% in 2 years.
After these steps if a company passes these filters I decide they are good enough to do research on. This is nowhere near the point I would buy.
All of these steps take practice and a lot of it. When you have looked at thousands of stocks you start to get a feel for industries, countries, and situations that can change your perspective.
Just think about how quickly Buffett could decide if a company was interesting or not. He had decades of experience so when any company came up he could reference the 50 others he had looked at with similar businesses at the same point in their cycle.
That is what they mean when they say knowledge compounds.
The only shortcut I know is subscribing so I do the research for you. Otherwise this takes time and a lot of work. 
For those that want to learn more about all the steps that come after click below.
For those that want to hire someone to do this for them subscribe below.
What I am Thinking About Today
Currently I am working on my ability to quickly assess companies using multiples. I had gotten complacent improving my process here until I listened to Li Lu’s Columbia presentation again.
It was a great reminder that the ability to quickly assess stocks is foundational to being an investor and I still have lots to learn.
Appreciate the time you spent reading and I will see you in the next one.

subject: He Got Fired From OpenAI at 22. Then He Turned $225M Into $5.5B by Betting on the AI Infrastructure No One Else Wa…
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://linas.substack.com/p/leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness-fund-portfolio-playbook

👋 Hey, Linas here! Every day, I break down 3 stories shaping the future of FinTech & Artificial Intelligence - plus the money movements and trends worth tracking. First time here? 370k+ FinTech and AI leaders get this daily. Join them:
Leopold Aschenbrenner is either the most important investor no one on Wall Street has heard of, or the most dangerous kind of genius: one who might actually be right. In the twelve months following the launch of his hedge fund, Situational Awareness LP, in September 2024, he grew its disclosed U.S. equity exposure from roughly $225 million to $5.52 billion 😳
He did it without owning a single share of Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, or Meta. His largest position was in a fuel-cell company. His second-largest was call options on a GPU cloud startup most investors had never heard of. His third-largest was call options on a chipmaker Wall Street had largely written off.
This is not a story about luck. It is a story about what happens when a mind trained in growth economics, existential risk theory, and AI scaling laws is given access to public markets and the conviction to act on conclusions everyone else considers too extreme to take seriously.
The Man Behind the Thesis
Leopold Aschenbrenner didn’t set out to run a hedge fund. He set out to understand how the world ends, and then figure out how to invest in the companies that would prevent it.
Born in Germany around 2001 to two medical doctors, he enrolled at Columbia University at fifteen. In 2021, at nineteen, he graduated as valedictorian with a double major in economics and mathematics-statistics, the same year he won a grant from Tyler Cowen’s Emergent Ventures. He did research at Oxford’s Global Priorities Institute alongside Philip Trammell, co-authoring a growth-economics paper that would later become the philosophical licence for his entire fund.
He interned at the FTX Future Fund, the philanthropic arm of Sam Bankman-Fried’s empire, and watched from the inside as one of the most spectacular coordination failures in recent financial history imploded. He resigned before the collapse. He then joined OpenAI’s Superalignment team in 2023, co-authored a paper on AI safety presented at a leading machine learning conference, and wrote an internal memo to the OpenAI board warning about Chinese espionage and the company’s security posture. OpenAI fired him in April 2024.
Two months later, he published Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, a 165-page essay series making a single sweeping claim: AGI is coming by 2027, the world is not ready, and the companies building the physical infrastructure to make it possible are the most undervalued assets in financial markets.
Ivanka Trump shared it. It went viral.
Within months, he raised anchor capital from Patrick and John Collison (Stripe co-founders), Daniel Gross, and Nat Friedman. One anchor LP told Fortune that Aschenbrenner pitched the fund by rejecting a venture-capital structure: AGI was going to be so consequential to the global economy that the only way to fully capitalise on it was to express investment ideas in the most liquid markets in the world. Public markets over private, because public markets scale with conviction and re-price faster.
Twelve months later, the fund’s 13F disclosed $5.52 billion in U.S. equity positions across 29 holdings. Let that sink in.
The Core Thesis
The One-Sentence Version: AGI is a 2027 event; superintelligence is a 2028–2030 event; the markets have not priced in either the exponential trendlines or the industrial mobilisation they require. Therefore: buy the bottlenecks of the buildout (power, compute, memory, optics, fabs) and short what AI eats.
What This Deep Dive Covers & Why It Matters
Most coverage of Leopold Aschenbrenner focuses on the headline number - 22-year-old, fired, now manages billions - and stops there. That framing is interesting but useless.
What actually matters is the architecture of thinking that generated those returns: the intellectual framework that turned a philosophical bet about artificial intelligence into one of the most concentrated, contrarian, and precisely sequenced portfolios in the hedge fund industry.
This deep dive goes several layers deeper:
The academic paper almost no one cites - a plain-English explanation of the Trammell-Aschenbrenner paper Existential Risk and Growth, co-authored with Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab, and why its core result (that the risk-minimising rate of technological growth is typically positive and often high) is the philosophical licence for the entire portfolio. It is the direct intellectual foundation for every position the fund has ever taken.
The 165-page manifesto decoded - the five core claims of Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, including the precise “Counting the OOMs” framework Aschenbrenner uses to forecast AGI by 2027, the three compounding vectors (compute, algorithmic efficiency, and “unhobbling”), and the specific test-time compute insight that explains the transition from chatbot to drop-in remote worker.
Quarter-by-quarter portfolio evolution - five quarters of 13F data dissected, from the first $254.8M, six-holding filing in Q4 2024 to the $5.52B, 29-holding book filed in February 2026. When did he pivot from semiconductors to power to Bitcoin miners? Why did he simultaneously short the entire semiconductor sector while remaining long Intel and Broadcom? And the DeepSeek moment in January 2025 - when everyone else panicked, and he bought.
The full portfolio breakdown - every position mapped to its thesis layer (electrons, compute, silicon, optics, memory, shorts), the activist 13D stake in Core Scientific, the Intel call-options bet decoded, the Bloom Energy fuel-cell play that Oracle just validated at 2.8 gigawatts, and the two private market moves the 13F doesn’t show.
A live portfolio tracker - a tool I built with Perplexity Computer [ https://substack.com/redirect/1a2becad-5d6e-426a-a58a-76cb3b4682b1?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ] to track Situational Awareness LP’s positions in real time as new 13F filings drop, along with the whole prompt to recreate it yourself.
The seven-rule reusable playbook - the complete framework, distilled from the thesis, the filings, and all available transcripts, that any investor, founder, or operator can apply to any technology S-curve, not just AI. The same logic that identified power companies and Bitcoin miners as the 2024–2025 winners can be applied to find the 2026–2028 equivalents - in robotics, in synthetic biology, in the physical supply chains of whatever comes after large language models.
The honest risk register - six specific ways this thesis breaks down (including the 14:1 implied leverage ratio most coverage never mentions), and the six signposts you should be watching to know whether it’s still working.
Every major technology wave has a set of physical constraints that are obvious in retrospect but invisible to most market participants in real time. Aschenbrenner made them visible - and bet on them before the crowd arrived.
Understanding exactly how he did that is worth more than any single stock tip.

subject: The Fundraising Cheat Code Most Founders Discover Too Late
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://www.the-founders-corner.com/p/the-fundraising-cheat-code-most-founders

There’s a number that should stop every founder in their tracks: 95%.
That’s the percentage of cold investor outreach that generates zero reply. Not a no. Silence.
Meanwhile, warm introductions convert at 58% or higher. That’s a 10–20× difference.
The founders who close rounds fast aren’t better at pitching. They’re better at preparation. They started the relationship before they needed the money, and by the time they officially opened a round, they weren’t convincing strangers - they were inviting people who already believed in them.
This article is the exact playbook for doing that. Six months of deliberate, light-touch work that means when you finally say “we’re raising,” half the room already wants in.
Also included at the end: the full Investor CRM you need to run this system - ready to copy and use today.
Why timing is the most under-rated fundraising variable
Most first-time founders treat fundraising like a sprint: build a deck, get warm intros, take 50 meetings, close a round. The problem is that model assumes investors are ready to move the moment you are.
They aren’t.
Venture capital decision-making is relationship-driven. Investors often commit to founders they’ve been tracking for months - watching them execute, hit milestones, and handle setbacks. There’s a concept in VC that captures this perfectly: investors invest in lines, not dots. A single meeting gives them one data point. Six months of consistent updates gives them a trajectory.
The data reinforces the timeline pressure. Carta’s 2025 State of Private Markets confirms seed valuations hit all-time highs - but deal counts fell 28% year-over-year. Fewer deals, higher competition, longer wait times between rounds. The median company in 2025 waited 1.9 years between seed and Series A - the longest recorded interval. Investors are more selective than at any point since 2018.
The other reality: early-stage rounds typically take three to six months from first meeting to wire. If you start building relationships at the same time you open the round, you’re looking at nine months minimum of cash runway consumed before a single penny arrives. Starting six months earlier means your raise isn’t racing against your runway - it’s an exercise in choosing between competing term sheets.
The Pre-Raise Framework: Month by Month
Here’s the full system, broken into three two-month phases.
Months 1–2: Build your target list and make first contact
The goal: Get on the radar of 50–75 relevant investors. Not pitch them. Not ask for anything. Just exist in their awareness.
Step 1: Build a tiered investor list
Most founders build their list wrong. They Google “top VCs” and start emailing Sequoia. This is how you waste three months.
Your investor list should be built around four filters, in this order:
1. Stage fit. A pre-seed fund cannot write a Series A cheque. An early-stage fund that’s already deployed 90% of its current vehicle isn’t writing any cheque. Research which funds are actively deploying at your stage. Crunchbase Pro (around £60–80/month) lets you filter by fund stage, recent investment activity, and check size. The fastest raisers use the most targeted lists.
2. Sector fit. Over 70% of active seed funds in 2025 focus on specific verticals. An investor with no B2B SaaS portfolio companies will not suddenly lead your B2B SaaS round. Filter by portfolio companies, not fund name.
3. Geography. Many European and UK funds cannot invest in non-UK entities. Many US funds won’t lead European rounds. Know the rules before you spend time on an investor.
4. Warm path. For every investor on your list, score them by how easily you can get an introduction. Check LinkedIn for second-degree connections. Use NFX Signal (free), which maps your Gmail and LinkedIn network against 14,000+ VC relationships, to surface invisible intro paths.
We built a tool specifically for this filtering process. Before you build your list manually, run it through our investor fit filter first - it matches your stage, sector, geography, and raise amount against 2,500+ active investors and surfaces only the ones who are structurally capable of saying yes. → Use The Quiet Filter here [ https://substack.com/redirect/a82f0f9a-df6a-4ae0-8717-81af384fc925?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ]
Aim for 75–100 names. Tier them:
Tier 1 (15–20): dream leads - high fit, warm intro path exists
Tier 2 (30–40): strong fits - sector and stage match, intro path requires work
Tier 3 (20–30): good options if Tiers 1–2 don’t convert
Build your tracking spreadsheet with these columns: Fund name, Partner name, Stage focus, Sector focus, Geography, Check size range, Warm intro path, and a “Why us” column. If you can’t write a sentence explaining why this specific investor would care about your company, remove them from the list.
Step 2: Make first contact - the permission ask
Here is the email that starts everything. It is not a pitch. It is a request for permission to stay in touch.
Subject: [Your Company] - mind if I share occasional updates?
Hi [Name],
I’m [Your Name], founder of [Company]. We’re building [one-sentence description] - we’re currently at [brief traction signal, e.g. £40K MRR, 3,200 active users, or “launching with 12 paying design partners”].
I saw your investment in [specific portfolio company] and thought you might find our progress interesting to follow. We’re not raising right now, but I’m planning to open a Seed round in [approximate month/quarter].
Would you mind if I added you to a short monthly update I send to a handful of people I’d love to have in our corner?
[Your Name]
Three things make this email work. First, you’re not asking for a meeting - the perceived cost is near zero. Second, you’ve demonstrated you know their portfolio. Third, you’ve flagged you’ll eventually raise, so they understand the context without feeling sold to.
The reply rate on this format is high. Early-stage VCs and angels almost universally say yes. Their job is to track emerging companies. You’re making that job easier.
Send this to your Tier 1 list in month one. Send it to Tier 2 in month two. Keep Tier 3 for when you officially open the round.
Months 3–4: The monthly investor update
This is where most founders quit. And it’s where the real work happens.
Once someone has agreed to receive updates, you need to deliver. Every month. Without fail.
Visible.vc’s data on this is unambiguous: founders who send consistent investor updates are twice as likely to raise follow-on funding from their current investors. NFX puts the same figure even higher - their survey of 870+ founders found that monthly updates are the single highest-value communication ritual a founder can build. The mechanism is simple - an investor who has watched you execute for five months has seen far more than an investor who hears a one-hour pitch.
We wrote a full deep-dive on crafting investor updates that actually get read and acted on - including the exact structure, what to include in each section, and the specific framing that turns passive investors into active allies: → Stop Sending Boring Investor Updates - Do This Instead [ https://substack.com/redirect/ae980d1e-f51a-4e0e-bd4d-8879e1cf2c66?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ]
The pre-raise monthly update template (keep it under 400 words):
Subject: [Company] - [Month] Update
Hi [First Name],
[One-sentence summary of where we stand.]
HEADLINE THIS MONTH [One specific, concrete win. Numbers preferred. “Closed our first enterprise customer at £2,400/month.” “Hit 1,000 active users.” “Signed LOI with [recognisable brand].”]
KEY METRICS → MRR: £[X] ([+X%] MoM) → Active users / customers: [X] → Burn rate: £[X]/month → Runway: [X] months
WHAT WE LEARNED [One honest insight or challenge. Founders who share what’s hard earn more trust than those who only share wins.]
WHAT’S NEXT [Two or three specific goals for next month. These become the metrics you report in the next update.]
ASK (optional, but powerful) [One specific ask - not “any intros would be great.” Instead: “If you know anyone at a Series A B2B SaaS fund actively looking at infrastructure tools, I’d love a connection.”]
[Your Name]
Send on the first Tuesday or Wednesday of the month - early-week is when investor inboxes are active and they’re at their desks, not in meetings or travel.
The power of this format is compounding. By month six, an investor who has received five of these updates has watched you state goals and hit them. They’ve seen you handle a setback honestly. They’ve tracked the revenue number growing. When you email them to say the round is open, they’re not starting from zero - they’re already halfway to a yes.
The rest of this playbook is for premium subscribers.
What’s inside:
The exact email sequences for converting warm relationships into committed investors - word for word, ready to send
The follow-up cadence that creates momentum without burning bridges, including the specific timing and triggers that move investors from warm to decided
How to handle the “not right now” reply in a way that keeps the door open and often generates your most valuable introductions
The 48-hour launch playbook for opening your round; how to create competing conversations from day one and use parallel momentum to close faster
The complete Investor CRM: six working tabs covering your master list, outreach log, monthly update tracker, active pipeline, intro map, and live dashboard
Premium subscribers also unlock The Founders Corner's full library of 50+ tools, templates, and deep-dives: investor lists, fundraising models, cap table templates, pitch deck frameworks, and every premium playbook published to date.
Keep reading with a 7-day free trial → [ https://substack.com/redirect/1b403ed1-0387-425a-8757-d4881e62c7d8?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ] Cancel anytime.

subject: Flash Note: Defense Production Act
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://www.citriniresearch.com/p/flash-note-defense-production-act

We have long spoken about how power is the most obvious intersection between our two largest themes of the decade. This is a brief update on the longstanding trend.
As a reminder, those themes are Fiscal Primacy and Artificial Intelligence. Fiscal Primacy is our core view that government priorities and spending are increasingly driving equity performance and crowding-in of capital. AI, of course, needs no explanation.
On April 20, the President signed the Presidential Determination 2026-10 [ https://substack.com/redirect/3e010963-e280-464a-932c-d642af719bbc?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ], a Defense Production Act (DPA) Section 303 determination for grid infrastructure, equipment, and supply-chain capacity.
“On January 20, 2025, I issued Executive Order 14156 (Declaring a National Energy Emergency), under the National Emergencies Act. That order found that America’s inadequate energy production, transportation, and infrastructure constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the Nation’s economy, national security, and foreign policy [...]
The Nation’s capacity to design, produce, and deploy large-scale grid infrastructure, including transformers, high-voltage transmission components, advanced conductors, power electronics, substations, and grid-supporting manufacturing equipment, is dangerously limited.”
The text formally classifies transformers, transmission lines, conductors, substations, high-voltage circuit breakers, power control electronics, protective relay systems, capacitor banks, and electrical core steel as essential to national defense.
We have been long this supply chain in various forms since 2023. We expanded on the idea in The Utility of Bubbles: The Intersection of Fiscal & AI [ https://substack.com/redirect/53a4583a-64de-49fd-a4d9-8140da0a5a21?j=eyJ1IjoiOGFiMHN3In0.zP6ncAt57e5BSjUJ_SVakLp2EJCK6mdxH_GkAgT_Z5c ] in June 2024. And the market has been pricing in this thesis since transformer lead times first crossed eighteen months.
The reality though, is that even after years of upward revisions, the grid backlog only continues to grow. In 1Q26, the quarterly net addition to GE Vernova’s (GEV US) electrification segment backlog was nearly as large as the annual additions from 2022-2025. Growth is accelerating, not abating.
Across grid infrastructure, transformers are a particularly acute bottleneck, especially given the historical reliance on Chinese producers. Friendlier suppliers are seeing record backlogs and have announced US capacity expansions.
The marginal supplier of large power transformers to the US grid is Korean. Hyosung Heavy Industries’ (298040 KS) Memphis plant is the only US facility capable of producing 765 kV ultra-high voltage transformers. HD Hyundai Electric (267260 KS) is expanding its Montgomery, AL production capacity with a new plant, bringing its total capacity to 150 units per year by 2027. LS Electric (010120 KS) just opened in Bastrop, TX. Iljin Electric (103590 KS), the smallest of the four, has recently broken into Western markets with its first European ultra-high-voltage transformer contract and a record $333M order from a US energy company.
The Korean Big Four combined order backlog sits at $23.9B as of Q3 2025, representing five to six years of work.
The bottleneck is great enough to warrant a national security concern and DPA action. Likewise, we think it’s valuable to revisit exactly where the winners are in that supply chain.
But first, what does the DPA order actually do?...

subject: Peter Boockvar | Nobody Special | Geoff Garbacz | Ross Hendricks.
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://georgenoble.substack.com/p/peter-boockvar-nobody-special-geoff

1. Strategic Actions and Decisions
Reduce Exposure to Semiconductors Ahead of Hyperscaler Earnings: The AI trade is “completely splintered.” While semis are winning, the hyperscalers (Meta, Google) spending on them face deteriorating cash flows. If these companies announce they are “just maintaining” rather than increasing CapEx this week, it will be a “catalyst to sell off the semis.” [01:36]
Delay Any Investment in Small Modular Reactors (SMRs): Despite data center companies hinting at building their own power, “there is still not a single licensed small modular reactor design in the United States.” It remains “illegal to build any of them for power generation,” and NRC approval moves at the “speed of continental drift.” [04:02]
Prepare for a 60-70% Downside in Specific Semiconductor Names: One speaker explicitly states he expects his clients’ holdings in names like “Sanders” to “fall by 60, 70% before this is all over.” The cyclical nature of semis guarantees a major bust following the current boom. [13:00]
Rotate into Energy and Commodities on Pullbacks: Even if the Middle East war ends, “85 is the new 65” for oil. Global hoarding to refill strategic reserves and rework supply chains will create a “multi-year” bid under commodities. One speaker specifically likes “noble the driller and some natural gas companies.” [26:31]
Do Not Assume a V-Shaped Recovery or Fed Rescue: The post-GFC playbook of buying every dip is broken because central banks are in an inflationary world. Their “hands are tied” preventing the ability to cut rates or use QE to create a “V bottom” like in previous downturns. [01:00:17]
2. Executive Summary
In this recording, my guests and I broke down a market that is completely nonsensical right now. Peter explained how the AI tech trade has splintered, with semis exhibiting “1999-type behavior” while software falls through the floor. We warned that this is an extraordinarily cyclical group—big booms are always followed by major busts. Jack brought a critical on-the-ground reality check, highlighting how states like Wisconsin are forcing data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades, and noted that up to 40% of planned builds are already delayed. Geoff backed this up with short interest data showing semis at all-time highs with no covering pressure. Ross reinforced our commodity thesis, arguing that even if the war ends, oil’s floor is now $85. The through-line was clear: valuations don’t matter until they do, and the post-2008 “buy the dip” playbook is broken in today’s inflationary world. 
3. Key Takeaways and Practical Lessons
1. The “V-Bottom” Playbook is Obsolete in an Inflationary Regime: Investors trained to buy every dip assume infinite Fed stimulus. That era is over because central banks cannot cut rates or restart QE meaningfully with current inflation.
Practical Lesson: Do not assume a quick recovery in tech drawdowns. Supply-driven shocks require patience, not dip-buying heroics.
2. Price-to-Sales Matters More Than P/E in Cyclical Peaks: Valuing a semi-company on one year of inflated earnings is a “mistake.” When gross margins are elevated but unsustainable, price-to-sales provides a clearer picture of risk.
Practical Lesson:  Before buying a stock trading at 6x book, calculate its price-to-sales and compare it to historical norms, not just its low P/E ratio.
3. Watch the Back End of the Oil Curve, Not the Front Month: Oil stocks did not rally as much as front-month crude because markets trade on long-term futures. The real move comes when back-end prices rise.
Practical Lesson: To enter a commodity trade, monitor the 12-36 month futures curve. A rising back end signals a structural shift, not just a geopolitical spike.
4. Construction Logistics Are the Leading Indicator for Semis: The AI bottleneck is no longer chips; it is transformers, aluminum, and permits. Up to 40% of planned data centers are delayed for these reasons.
Practical Lesson: Monitor industrial construction metrics (transformer lead times, permitting rulings in states like Wisconsin) as the true leading indicator for semiconductor demand.
5. Separate Technological Miracles from Business Viability: SpaceX is “freaking incredible” technologically, but its IPO valuation relies on a “self-referential” $28 trillion TAM cited by Elon Musk without evidence.
Practical Lesson:  When evaluating IPOs like SpaceX, ignore the engineering superlatives and demand audited financials. If the TAM is self-reported by the CEO, treat it as marketing, not data

subject: The Empire Unmasked: Elite Impunity and the Slow Collapse of American Legitimacy
full_body:
View this post on the web at https://georgenoble.substack.com/p/the-empire-unmasked-elite-impunity

American power is seriously frayed, but still intact; American legitimacy is not, and legitimacy is what makes power sustainable.
For most of its history, the United States has justified its power—at home and abroad—through a cluster of myths: impartial rule of law, meritocratic opportunity, fair markets, and a liberal international order grounded in universal principles rather than naked interest. Those myths were never fully true. But they were plausible enough that citizens could half‑believe them and allies could treat American leadership as something more than brute force.
That plausibility is collapsing in real time. The problem is not that corruption exists; it always has. The problem is that it is visible, normalized, and unpunished in precisely those sectors that claim to anchor legitimacy: federal law enforcement, high finance, the presidency, and the “rules‑based” global order. The United States still has enormous residual power--military, financial, technological; but its ideological credit line is being run down faster than it is being replenished.
We are not watching the sudden fall of Rome. We are watching something more subtle: a widening mismatch between the myths America tells about itself and the observable behavior of its ruling strata. This essay makes a simple claim, in three moves: first, how elite impunity works; second, how it has been built into law and oversight; and third, what that does to domestic cohesion and international order.
Mechanism: Elite Impunity as the New Normal
Start with the basic pattern: enough accountability theater to preserve institutional dignity, not enough accountability to threaten the networks that matter.
The Epstein saga has become a kind of Rosetta Stone for understanding how the United States handles crimes that implicate its upper echelons. A sprawling network of abuse and compromise, dense with billionaires, donors, academics, and politicians was ultimately reduced to one dead man in federal custody in 2019, a single high‑profile accomplice, and years of partial disclosure.
Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?-- Juvenal
Whatever one thinks of any individual name in the released material, the public takeaway has been consistent: the documents suggest broad elite proximity to Epstein, while the enforcement outcome remains narrowly bounded. The new moniker “The Epstein Class” has gained universal usage because it is very true. The sickness is becoming more broadly accepted as far more pervasive and perverse than anyone admitted only a few years ago. What has become accepted is still likely just scratching the surface of a very large, ugly iceberg. The established system can only disclose enough to signal seriousness yet still not converge on closure because the bar for additional prosecutions in elite‑implicating cases is effectively “perfect evidence,” not “persuasive pattern.” The inner sanctum of the uber elites is increasingly seen as thoroughly corrupt and beyond the rule of law. This is not only the stuff of collapse, it is the fuel for revolution.
A similar dynamic appears in markets. Multiple investigations have noted clusters of uncannily well‑timed trades, index futures, oil options, concentrated equity bet placed shortly before surprise presidential announcements on tariffs, sanctions, military action, or public signals that sent prices lurching. Each trade, taken alone, can be explained as aggressive speculation in a volatile environment. In aggregate, the pattern is hard to distinguish from systematic advantage tied to political access, yet the standard for proving criminal insider trading is high enough that “everyone can see it” and “we can prosecute it” rarely converge.
But it is not only the greed, unethicality and immorality of the self-dealing within the American government and the elite circles of sycophants that thrive in its wake, it is the blatant, in your face arrogance that is creating a tipping point domestically and in other similar ruling Western powers where the ability to recover legitimacy and faith will soon become virtually impossible.
This produces an epistemic trap: what an intelligent observer can infer is far ahead of what the legal system will formally acknowledge. Legitimacy fails in the gap between what’s obvious and what can be enforced. The lack of even displaying a willingness to abide by the clearly dying myth of the rule of law, or even to go through the motions of doing so, is an undertow to the entire American system of governance that could soon rip the nation apart.
You can feel it at ground level. A contractor who mis-bills a government program faces swift audits, claw backs, and potentially prison; a local official who takes a crude envelope of cash can be prosecuted; an ordinary defendant can be crushed by process. Meanwhile, the most consequential forms of corruption, the kind routed through foundations, consulting retainers, board seats, “speaking” fees, deniable access, and gross self-dealing in the billions of dollars, live in a zone where investigators hesitate, statutes narrow, and proof standards rise until the case becomes politically or legally impossible.
We are thus in a peculiar epistemic situation: everyone can see the structure of elite enrichment and impunity, but almost nothing can be “proven” to the legal standards that would make it punishable. The gap between what any intelligent observer can infer and what the system is willing to recognize as criminal is now the core of the legitimacy problem.
This is not only a story about timid prosecutors. It is the predictable outcome of an architecture that has been rewritten to raise the floor under elite behavior. American power is intact; American legitimacy is not, and that is the vulnerability rivals and demagogues can both exploit. It signals that the denouement is near.
Consequences: From Liberal Republic to Late Empire, Inevitably-Collapse.
Seen in isolation, each of these developments could be filed under “bad trends” or “troubling cases.” Taken together, they look less like discrete episodes and more like the signature of the regime transitions that put the final nail in the coffin of any semblance of democratic rule.
Internally, this produces the mood many of us now recognize: a mix of angry clarity and exhausted resignation. People see that the game is rigged, understand that the law does not bind the ruling class in any meaningful way, and oscillate between futile reformism, nihilistic withdrawal, and support for anti‑system figures who promise catharsis rather than repair.
Externally, it produces something even more consequential: the exhaustion of American exceptionalism as a credible story.
Hypocrisy, Hegemony, and the End of the Liberal Order
For roughly three generations after 1945, American primacy rested on a combination of material superiority and a persuasive narrative: U.S. leadership served a liberal international order that, while imperfect and often self‑serving, nonetheless generated real public goods, security guarantees, open trade, development finance, partial constraint on naked aggression. That “rules‑based order” story was, a supportive myth, a meme powerful enough that even critics had to take it seriously.
That is no longer the case. Analysts now describe the fracturing of the U.S.-led liberal international order, driven not only by the rise of China and the assertiveness of Russia, but by U.S. behavior itself: episodic dictatorial unilateralism, weaponization of sanctions, trade wars, visible double standards on sovereignty and human rights, and an increasingly blatantly overt, almost desperate attempt to undermine any perceived competitor. Thucydides Trap on steroids!
Scholars of international legitimacy speak increasingly of the “hypocrisy charge”: the accusation that Western states, the United States above all, proclaim universal liberal norms while violating them whenever convenient. This charge is no longer the province of anti‑American radicals; it appears routinely in mainstream analyses of the post‑Iraq, post‑financial crisis, and the post 25 years of external aggression by the weakening American Empire. This has become a tsunami under the new Trumpian order, a tsunami whose undertow is rapidly eroding the sands of legitimacy upon which America once stood firmly.
The key point is not that hypocrisy exists; all great powers are hypocritical. It is that the gap between American rhetoric and American practice has become so wide, so visible, and so uncorrected that the myths underpinning U.S. leadership no longer function as a convincing supportive device. Allies still cooperate with Washington out of necessity, habit, and fear of alternatives; adversaries exploit the gap relentlessly. But few outside the United States are under any illusion that U.S. power is bound by the rules it espouses. Once the American Empire commanded through the soft power of respect, admiration and emulation. This is has ended to be replaced with force, fear and uncertainty.
The visible domestic impunity of U.S. elites; no accountability for torture, for the architects of the 2008 crisis, for sprawling influence‑peddling networks, for the full extent of Epstein’s clientele, for the obvious insider enrichment around presidential policy tweets, feeds directly into this external perception. A state that does not hold its own ruling class to account will not be believed when it claims to uphold a principled order abroad. Both domestic and international observers are losing belief in all that America once held itself up to be.
The Dollar as Barometer of Trust
The same story shows up in the financial system. Dollar hegemony has been the monetary expression of American centrality since 1945, resting on a combination of economic weight, deep markets, and a baseline of political and legal trust. That hegemony is not collapsing overnight, but it is being slowly diluted.
The Trump war om Iran has dramatically failed. No matter the end result on the battlefield the Empires chessboard has been flipped and the pieces will lie in disarray never to be placed back on the board as it once was. The geopolitical dynamics of the Middle East will never return to even the prewar fragility of the Pax American and the Petrodollar. If current trends continue unabated, a sudden, unforeseen implosion of the currency is a possibility with obvious repercussions to the global economy and to the American hegemonic system.
Analysts now speak openly of a shift from dollar hegemony to currency multipolarity, as emerging powers seek alternatives in bilateral trade, central bank swaps, and new payment systems. The dollar’s dominance is being shaken not only by U.S. debt and fiscal politics, but by the perception that Washington has become increasingly willing to weaponize access to its financial system for short‑term geopolitical leverage.
These are not just technical adjustments. They reflect a quiet hedging against American governance risk: the sense that U.S. institutions are no longer as predictable, law‑bound, or self‑restraining as they once appeared. The “sell America” trade is not yet a stampede, but it exists in the discourse in a way it simply did not a decade ago.
From Legitimacy Erosion to Imperial Unraveling
Put these threads together, and a pattern emerges that looks uncanny like the late stages of previous hegemonic orders.
Domestically:
Legal norms at the top are being rewritten to narrow what counts as corruption and to insulate executive power from accountability.
Federal law enforcement remains powerful but is increasingly selective, robust against marginal actors and fragile when faced with complex elite networks.
High finance operates in a zone of de facto impunity, profiting from what look like systematic informational advantages tied to political power.
Citizens who can see this lose any deep belief that the law binds their rulers, and oscillate between anger, cynicism, and despair.
Internationally:
The liberal order narrative has been hollowed out by decades of selective application and is now openly questioned even in establishment fora.
Dollar centrality is being cautiously hedged as states explore alternative arrangements, not because they dislike liquidity, but because they fear political risk.
The hypocrisy charge has become a central lens for understanding U.S. behavior, undermining Washington’s claims to moral leadership, which was a sustaining myth to begin with.
Empires do not end because someone disproves their myths in academic articles. They end when the supporting myths cease to function as shared fictions that structure expectations and behavior—when neither the domestic population nor foreign partners treat them as even aspirationally true. At that point, what remains is force, habit, and inertia.
The United States is unlikely to experience a sudden, cinematic collapse. Far more plausible is a drawn‑out imperial unravelling:
a hollowing‑out of institutions at home, where law becomes ever more nakedly an instrument of class and faction;
an oscillation between managerial oligarchy and spasms of populist catharsis that fail to reconstruct legitimacy;
a gradual fragmentation of the international order into overlapping, competing spheres of influence and financial circuits.
However the future unfolds, America must restrain its anachronistic hubris. If not, the world will suffer a far worse outcome than that resulting from the increasing vacuum from the waning American hegemonic rule.
In that context, elite impunity is not a side‑effect of decline; it is one of its primary mechanisms. Each non‑prosecution, each legalized “gratitude” payment, each “well‑timed trade” that goes unexamined, each buried oversight report, each unpunished network of abuse, all of them communicate the same message: the rules are for you, not for us. The same stands for the appearance of the blatant extortionist policies internationally now being persued by the Trump Imperium. Over time, that message erodes the belief that the system is reformable, that there is any point in treating its promises as binding.
You can stand on that threshold and still argue that reform is possible, and that new coalitions, institutional redesign, and external shocks could push the United States back toward a more republican equilibrium. Or you can conclude, as many quietly have, that we are already in the early stages of a long, painful, cathartic abyss; a process in which the empire’s myths come apart faster than its power, leaving a dangerous interval of decadence, volatility, and improvisation.
Either way, the first step is to name the situation clearly. The American polity is no longer suffering from isolated scandals or partisan excess. It is suffering from a systemic collapse of elite accountability, and with it, the slow death of the narratives that once justified its dominance.
Once trust and belief disappear, they are virtually impossible to recover. Despite the absurd level of propaganda from the waning Empire, admitting reality is the most important step to finding a more stable equilibrium without which chaos awaits.

eToro stopped being just a broker, and nobody noticed 😳💸
The news 🗞️ One of the most consequential moves in retail finance this month wasn’t a rate decision or an IPO filing. It was eToro quietly shipping an App Store.
Let’s unpack this.
More on this 👉 WealthTech eToro just opened a marketplace where anyone - developers, quants, Pro Investors, or non-technical traders using AI “vibe coding”- can build and publish apps that plug directly into live trading infrastructure.
Algorithmic execution, social analytics, portfolio rebalancing, AI-managed sub-accounts: all accessible via API, MCP server, or natural-language prompts.
By launch day, 800+ Pro Investors had already built over 1,000 tools. Users install with one click through SSO. No separate logins, no data migration.
Zoom out 🔎 The playbook is obvious because it’s proven. Apple, Salesforce, Shopify all made the same bet: the platform that attracts the most builders captures the most users and becomes nearly impossible to leave. eToro is running that play against a competitive set - Robinhood, Interactive Brokers, Schwab - that either lacks a marketplace entirely or serves one aimed at professionals.
IBKR’s Investor’s Marketplace lists 1,500+ services but targets experienced traders. Bloomberg’s Open API costs $24,000/year per terminal. eToro is handing equivalent capabilities to 40 million registered users for free, then letting the community iterate faster than any internal product team could.
The timing is also tighter than it looks. Agent Portfolios launched in March (autonomous AI trading with $200 minimums, new registrations up 30% in Q1). Tori, eToro’s AI companion, just got Grok 4.2 integration and persistent memory. Then there’s the $70 million Zengo acquisition that gives eToro self-custodial wallet infrastructure for tokenized assets and prediction markets.
The App Store is the connective layer that turns these from features into a platform. And platforms usually win.
THE TAKEAWAY ✈️
What’s next? 🤔 Looking ahead, here’s what you should watch. First and foremost, the financial impact is back-loaded: retention and trading volume compound slowly, but the lock-in mechanics are real. Every installed app, every configured agent strategy, every follower relationship makes switching more painful. If eToro captures even modest developer energy, it creates a data flywheel - millions of live AI strategies generating proprietary behavioral datasets - that no competitor can replicate by copying the product. The risk is obviously curation. A flood of poorly built tools that lose people money turns the App Store from a moat into a liability, and regulators in the US and EU will be paying attention the moment AI agents start executing trades at scale. eToro’s current legal framing as “neutral technology infrastructure” is clever positioning, but it won’t survive contact with the first high-profile retail loss driven by a vibe-coded algo. Thus, the real question here isn’t whether eToro can launch an app store. It’s whether brokerage competitors can respond before the developer lock-in sets. Interesting times ahead 👀
